Locality-Induced Hierarchical Backflow Wavefunctions for Correlated Fermions

Yu-Tong Zhou Affiliation: Anhui Province Key Laboratory of Quantum Network, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China Affiliation: Synergetic Innovation Center of Quantum Information and Quantum Physics, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China Affiliation: Hefei National Laboratory, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230088, China    Zheng-Wei Zhou Email: zwzhou@ustc.edu.cn Affiliation: Anhui Province Key Laboratory of Quantum Network, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China Affiliation: Synergetic Innovation Center of Quantum Information and Quantum Physics, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China Affiliation: Hefei National Laboratory, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230088, China Affiliation: Anhui Center for Fundamental Sciences in Theoretical Physics, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China    Wen-Yuan Liu Email: wyliu@zju.edu.cn Affiliation: Institute for Advanced Study in Physics and School of Physics, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310027, China
Abstract

We show that locality provides a natural principle to hierarchically organize backflow wavefunctions. This leads us to propose a family of variational fermionic states, termed hierarchical backflow (HB) wavefunctions. The expressive power of HB is systematically improvable, controlled by a path depth KK which reflects the range of backflow correlations. At half-filling, the HB with K=1K=1 already achieves high energy precision, with an accuracy around 0.5%0.5\% for system sizes from 4×44\times 4 to 10×1010\times 10. At hole doping nh=0.125n_{h}=0.125, the method scales efficiently to 12×1612\times 16 and 16×1616\times 16 systems, and the energy systematically achieves higher accuracy with KK increasing, yielding a clear stripe phase. The HB further enables a local-nonlocal decomposition, naturally bridging to neural quantum states, while featuring compact representations and efficient optimization. Our work reveals locality as a natural organizing principle of backflow wavefunctions, opening a new framework with systematic improvability and interpretability for large-scale simulations of correlated fermion systems.

Introduction. Simulating and representing strongly correlated fermionic systems is a central task in condensed matter physics. These systems host many extraordinary phenomena such as high-temperature superconductivity, Mott transitions, quantum magnetism [18, 13, 12, 7, 16, 9, 45, 2], yet accurately characterizing their nature presents a fundamental challenge due to the exponentially large Hilbert space. To overcome this difficulty, a variety of powerful approaches have been developed, such as dynamical mean-field theory [14, 21, 22], quantum Monte Carlo [46, 47, 37, 42, 1, 39] and tensor network methods [44, 43, 20, 15, 23, 36, 5, 6, 26, 29, 27, 28, 30], each offering distinct insights and capabilities. Nevertheless, due to this complexity, developing efficient and systematically improvable methods remains an urgent need.

In recent years, neural network quantum states have provided a promising approach to simulate correlated fermion systems. Most such states are built upon backflow wavefunctions [33, 34, 4, 24, 3, 31, 49, 32, 25], introduced by Feynman and Cohen in 1956 to describe liquid helium [11]. A backflow wavefunction encodes the fermion sign structure by taking the form of Slater determinants, but with each single-particle orbital depending on the configuration of all other particles, a property known as backflow correlations. This allows it to capture many-body physics beyond the mean-field level while preserving fermionic antisymmetry. Yet despite its 70-year history, a clear organizing principle underlying the expressive power of backflow wavefunctions remains lacking. Existing approaches, though expressive, typically treat the configuration dependence of the orbitals as generic global functions, posing challenges for systematic interpretability, improvement, and optimization.

In this work, we reveal that locality provides a natural organizing principle that builds backflow correlations from iterated local transitions, rather than viewing it as a mysterious nonlocal feature. This perspective leads to a new family of variational fermionic states, which we term hierarchical backflow (HB) wavefunctions. Their expressive power is controlled by a path depth KK, reflecting the locality-induced hierarchical structure of backflow correlations. For K=0K=0, the ansatz reduces to the Hartree-Fock state, while increasing KK systematically improves the expressive power. Furthermore, the hierarchical backflow naturally leads to a local-nonlocal decomposition that bridges directly to neural network quantum states, enabling compact representations compared to conventional global-network architecture.

We demonstrate this framework on the two-dimensional Hubbard model. At half-filling, even with the smallest nontrivial depth K=1K=1, the HB already achieves high energy precision, with a relative energy error around 0.5%0.5\% for system sizes from 4×44\times 4 to 10×1010\times 10. At hole doping n=0.125n=0.125, scaling to 12×1612\times 16 and 16×1616\times 16, the energy progressively improves to higher accuracy with increasing KK, exhibiting a clear stripe phase. Our work thus establishes locality as a natural organizing principle of backflow wavefunctions, opening a new systematically improvable and interpretable framework for large-scale simulations of strongly correlated fermion systems.

Locality-induced hierarchy in backflows. Consider a fermionic Hubbard-type Hamiltonian with nearest-neighbor interactions on an NN-site lattice:

H=∑⟨i​j⟩ti​j​ci†​cj+∑⟨i​k⟩Ui​k​ni​nk,H=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}t_{ij}c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}+\sum_{\langle ik\rangle}U_{ik}n_{i}n_{k}, (1)

where ci†c_{i}^{\dagger} (cic_{i}) are fermionic creation (annihilation) operators at site ii (spin indices suppressed for simplifying notation), and ni=ci†​cin_{i}=c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{i} is the particle number operator.

We first introduce the necessary notation. Let |𝐬⟩=|s1s2⋯sN⟩|\mathbf{s}\rangle=|s_{1}s_{2}\cdots s_{N}\rangle denote a configuration in the occupation number basis, with si=0s_{i}=0 or 11 for spinless fermions at site ii. For an MM-particle |𝐬⟩|\mathbf{s}\rangle with an occupied site ii (si=1s_{i}=1), define 𝐬¯\bar{\mathbf{s}} as the background configuration of the remaining M−1M-1 electrons. Each pair (i,𝐬¯)(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) uniquely labels a configuration |𝐬⟩|\mathbf{s}\rangle. For example, if |𝐬⟩=|110101⟩|\mathbf{s}\rangle=|110101\rangle, then for i=2i=2, |𝐬¯⟩=|100101⟩|\bar{\mathbf{s}}\rangle=|100101\rangle.

A general fermionic wavefunction for an MM-electron system is |Φ⟩=∑𝐬W⁡(𝐬)​|𝐬⟩|\Phi\rangle=\sum_{\mathbf{s}}W(\mathbf{s})|\mathbf{s}\rangle. For a backflow wavefunction expressed as a Slater determinant, the amplitude W⁡(𝐬)W(\mathbf{s}) can be obained by expanding the determinant along the ii-th column for any occupied site ii:

W⁡(𝐬)=det(Ψ)=∑mψm​(i,𝐬¯)​Cm​(i,𝐬¯),W(\mathbf{s})=\det(\Psi)=\sum_{m}\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}), (2)

where the matrix element Ψm​i=ψm​(i,𝐬¯)\Psi_{mi}=\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is the backflow orbital, and Cm​(i,𝐬¯)C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is the corresponding (m,i)(m,i)-cofactor of the matrix Ψ\Psi [11, 41, 40]. The index m=1,…,Mm=1,\dots,M labels the orbitas. Unlike the Hartree-Fock approach, where orbitals depend only on single-particle coordinates, here each orbital ψm​(i,𝐬¯)\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) depends on the full background configuration of the remaining electrons.

The energy function E=⟨Φ|H|Φ⟩/⟨Φ|Φ⟩E=\langle\Phi|H|\Phi\rangle/\langle\Phi|\Phi\rangle is typically optimized variationally with respect to the backflow orbital parameters ψm​(i,𝐬¯)\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}). To gain insight into the structure of these orbitals, we motivate an effective single-particle-like eigenvalue problem (see Supplemental Material):

∑j[Hmeff​(𝐬¯)]i​j​ψm​(j,𝐬¯)=Em​(𝐬¯)​ψm​(i,𝐬¯),\sum_{j}\left[H_{m}^{\mathrm{eff}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\right]_{ij}\psi_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})=E_{m}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}), (3)

where the effective Hamiltonian elements read

[Hmeff​(𝐬¯)]i​j=1γm​(i,𝐬¯)​Cm​(j,𝐬¯)Cm​(i,𝐬¯)​(ti​j​ηi​jh​(𝐬¯)+δi​j​∑kUj​k​ηj​kI​(𝐬¯)),\left[H_{m}^{\mathrm{eff}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\right]_{ij}=\frac{1}{\gamma_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}\frac{C_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}{C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}\left(t_{ij}\eta^{\mathrm{h}}_{ij}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})+\delta_{ij}\sum_{k}U_{jk}\eta^{\mathrm{I}}_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\right), (4)

where Em​(𝐬¯)E_{m}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}) plays the role of an effective energy eigenvalue, γm​(i,𝐬¯)\gamma_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is a nonzero factor, and ηi​jh​(𝐬¯)\eta_{ij}^{\mathrm{h}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}) and ηj​kI​(𝐬¯)\eta^{\mathrm{I}}_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}) enforce that the hopping and interaction terms contribute only when the required sites are occupied appropriately. We restrict to configurations with Cm​(i,𝐬¯)≠0C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\neq 0, as others do not contribute. See Supplemental Material for details.

Note Eq. (4) is nonlinear and computationally challenging because HmeffH^{\mathrm{eff}}_{m} depends on the configuration of all other sites. To elucidate its structure, we make a local kernel approximation that retains only two-site contributions in which [Hmeff​(𝐬¯)]i​j[H^{\mathrm{eff}}_{m}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})]_{ij} depends only on the occupation variable at site ii and its nearest neighbor jj. Under this approximation, the effective Hamiltonian reduces to a local kernel Hmloc​(i,si,j,sj)H^{\mathrm{loc}}_{m}(i,s_{i};j,s_{j}) determined solely by the two site occupations.

This kernel defines local transitions between sites, with each transition element depending on the local variables sis_{i} and sjs_{j}. Iterating such kernel actions on an initial orbital (e.g., the Hartree-Fock orbital) therefore accumulates background information step by step, generating a nonlocal dependence on the full configuration, a natural manifestation of backflow correlations. The iterative structure can be expressed as a sum over paths of successive local transitions, reminiscent of the power method.

Motivated by this observation, we introduce a family of variational fermionic states termed hierarchical backflow (HB) wavefunctions, by parameterizing the backflow orbitals as a path expansion with depth KK:

ψmHB​(i,𝐬¯)=∑i1,…,iK∏l=1Kfm[l]​(il−1,sil−1,il,sil),\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})=\sum_{i_{1},\dots,i_{K}}\;\prod_{l=1}^{K}f_{m}^{[l]}(i_{l-1},s_{i_{l-1}};i_{l},s_{i_{l}}), (5)

with the initial site i≡i0i\equiv i_{0}. Each factor fm[l]f_{m}^{[l]} contains a set of variational parameters encoding how the orbital at the reference site il−1i_{l-1} is influenced by the occupations of its neighboring sites ili_{l}, thereby generating backflow correlations. The path depth KK defines the range of backflow correlations from a starting site ii and increasing KK systematically extends this range, providing a variational ansatz with controlled and systematically improvable expressive power.

For K=0K=0, the expansion reduces to a function depending only on ii (i.e., ψmHB​(i,𝐬¯)|K=0=ψmHF​(i)\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\big|_{K=0}=\psi^{\mathrm{HF}}_{m}(i)). This recovers the Hartree-Fock wavefunction, where the orbital is independent of the background 𝐬¯\bar{\mathbf{s}} and thus lack backflow correlations. The first-order expansion (K=1K=1) reads

ψmHB​(i,𝐬¯)|K=1=∑jfm[1]​(i,si,j,sj),\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\big|_{K=1}=\sum_{j}f_{m}^{[1]}(i,s_{i};j,s_{j}), (6)

and the second-order expansion (K=2K=2) is

ψmHB​(i,𝐬¯)|K=2=∑j,pfm[1]​(i,si,j,sj)​fm[2]​(j,sj,p,sp),\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\big|_{K=2}=\sum_{j,p}f_{m}^{[1]}(i,s_{i};j,s_{j})f_{m}^{[2]}(j,s_{j};p,s_{p}), (7)

where jj runs over ii and its four nearest neighbors, and pp runs over jj and its four nearest neighbors.

The wavefunction amplitude is then obtained as a Slater determinant of the HB orbitals, W⁡(𝐬)=det[ψmHB​(i,𝐬¯)]W(\mathbf{s})=\det\left[\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\right]. Notably, despite the small path depth KK, the Slater determinant couples all HB orbitals, generating many-body correlations in the amplitude W⁡(𝐬)W(\mathbf{s}).

One can also relax the two-site kernel approximation to higher-order local kernels, e.g., three-site kernels, leading to a three-site variant of the hierarchical backflow ansatz with factors fm[l]​(i,si,j,sj,p,sp)f_{m}^{[l]}(i,s_{i};\;j,s_{j};\;p,s_{p}). We expect that the two-site HB family with large KK have similar expressivity to the three-site family with small KK; for instance, the two-site construction with K=2K=2 closely resembles the three-site construction with K=1K=1 (up to a reparameterization). Here we always adopt the two-site HB family.

Effectiveness of the hierarchical backflow. We first examine the convergence of the HB ansatz with respect to the path depth KK. All calculations are performed using variational Monte Carlo with gradient-based optimization such as stochastic reconfiguration [38]. Figure 2(a) shows the KK-dependence of the energy for the half-filled Hubbard model on system sizes from 4×44\times 4 to 10×1010\times 10 with U=8U=8 under periodic boundary conditions (PBC), while Figure 2(b) shows the analogous results at hole doping nh=0.125n_{h}=0.125 for 4×L4\times L systems (L=4L=4 to 1616). We show results for K=0,1,2K=0,1,2. In all cases, the energy drops sharply from K=0K=0 (Hartree-Fock) to K=1K=1, and then improves modestly from K=1K=1 to K=2K=2. Remarkably, for half-filling, even K=1K=1 achieves relative energy errors as low as around 0.5%0.5\% across all system sizes from 4×44\times 4 to 10×1010\times 10 and interaction strengths U=2−8U=2-8, when benchmarked against unbiased auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) reference energies (see Table 1). This rapid convergence shows that the locality-induced hierarchy captures the vast majority of many-body correlations already at the shallow nontrivial depth. For the doped case, our K=1K=1 results already outperform existing neural-network-based backflow ansatze [33, 34] (see later), and increasing KK systematically pushes the energy even lower, which is a direct manifestation of the systematic improvability promised by our framework.

To further assess the quality of the correlations captured by the HB, we compute the staggered spin-spin correlation function C⁡(r)=(−1)x+y​⟨𝐒⁡(0,0)⋅𝐒⁡(x,y)⟩C(r)=(-1)^{x+y}\langle\mathbf{S}(0,0)\cdot\mathbf{S}(x,y)\rangle, where r=x2+y2r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} is the distance and 𝐒⁡(x,y)\mathbf{S}(x,y) is the spin operator at coordinate (x,y)(x,y). Figure 2(c) shows its behavior on a 10×1010\times 10 lattice. As a reference, we use the thermodynamic limit (TDL) magnetic moments from AFQMC evaluation [35]. Our 10×1010\times 10 results exhibit a similar UU-dependence to the TDL values. For instance, correlations are strongest at U=6U=6, and at both U=6U=6 and U=8U=8 they display clear long-range order, consistent with the well-known antiferromagnetic ground state at half-filling. Strikingly, all of this qualitatively correct physics, including the correct interaction strength for maximal order, is already captured by the K=1K=1 wavefunction.

We then scale to larger systems, including 12×1612\times 16 and 16×1616\times 16 lattices at hole doping nh=0.125n_{h}=0.125 and U=8U=8 under PBC. The ground state energies on the 16×1616\times 16 lattice are −0.5889-0.5889 (HB K=0K=0), −0.7510-0.7510 (HB K=1K=1) and −0.7526-0.7526 (HB K=2K=2), only about 0.2%0.2\% higher than the recent variational auxiliary-field Monte Carlo result of Sorella et al., −0.7544-0.7544 [39, 10]. Figure 3 presents the hole density and spin moment distributions using K=2K=2, which clearly reveal a stripe phase with wavelength λ=8\lambda=8, consistent with previous studies [9, 30]. These results demonstrate that HB scales efficiently to large system sizes (12×1612\times 16, 16×1616\times 16), systematically improves the energy with KK, and captures the stripe phase with wavelength λ=8\lambda=8, consistent with prior studies [48, 30].

Overall, these results establish HB as a systematically improvable and highly efficient approach for large-scale simulations of strongly correlated fermions.

Residual Hierarchical Backflow. The HB framework naturally enables a local-nonlocal decomposition, providing a direct bridge to neural network quantum states while preserving interpretable representation. By keeping the path depth KK small and incorporating residual correlations via an additional nonlocal factor, we construct a variant termed residual hierarchical backflow (RHB). The nonlocal part can be parameterized by a flexible function approximator (e.g., a neural network or a tensor network), while the HB backbone remains physically transparent and systematically improvable.

A convenient realization of RHB uses a multi-determinant construction in which all Slater determinants share the same HB orbitals ψmHB\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}, but each determinant carries its own nonlocal factor Qm[α]​(𝐬¯)Q_{m}^{[\alpha]}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}):

Ψm​i[α]=ψmHB​(i,𝐬¯)​Qm[α]​(𝐬¯),\Psi^{[\alpha]}_{mi}=\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\,Q_{m}^{[\alpha]}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}), (8)

and thus the amplitude is W⁡(𝐬)=∑αdet(Ψ[α])W(\mathbf{s})=\sum_{\alpha}\det(\Psi^{[\alpha]}), where α\alpha labels the Slater determinant.

Compared to conventional backflow architectures that rely on a single global network to directly generate orbital functions [33, 34, 31], the RHB representation is more compact (see End Matter) and can be optimized efficiently via a two-stage scheme (details in Supplemental Material). As an example, we instantiate the RHB with an HB K=2K=2 backbone and a feed-forward neural network (FNN) parameterizing Qm[α]​(𝐬¯)Q_{m}^{[\alpha]}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}). On the 16×1616\times 16 lattice at nh=0.125n_{h}=0.125 and U=8U=8, RHB with the FNN yields a ground state energy of −0.7543​(2)-0.7543(2), in excellent agreement with the aforementioned variational auxiliary-field Monte Carlo result −0.7544-0.7544 [39, 10], while the spin moment and hole density distributions remain essentially unchanged from the pure HB K=2K=2 results.

We further compare our approach with other backflow-based methods that employ a single global network: neural-network backflow (NNB) [33] and hidden-fermion determinant state (HFDS) [34]. All calculations are performed on 4×L4\times L lattices at nh=0.125n_{h}=0.125 and U=8U=8, shown in Figure 4. For the 4×44\times 4 system, both our RHB and HFDS agree excellently with exact diagonalization, with energy errors of approximately 0.00080.0008. On 4×84\times 8, our RHB energy is slightly lower than that of HFDS, and the improvement becomes more pronounced on larger lattices (e.g., 4×164\times 16). Remarkably, even the simplest HB with K=1K=1 already outperforms NNB across all system sizes, and increasing to K=2K=2 or using RHB yields further improvements. These results highlight the flexibility of the HB framework and the advantage of its local-nonlocal structure.

Conclusions. Although the backflow wavefunction was proposed about 70 years ago, its underlying organizing principle has remained elusive. In this work, we reveal that locality provides such a natural organizing principle, inducing a hierarchical structure controlled by a path depth KK. The resulting HB wavefunction smoothly interpolates from the Hartree-Fock state (K=0K=0) to increasingly correlated states (K>0K>0), offering a clear physical interpretation of backflow correlations. It also admits a local-nonlocal decomposition, where the nonlocal component can be chosen flexibly, such as a convolutional neural network, a tensor network or a Jastrow factor. This flexibility makes HB a versatile backbone for designing expressive yet interpretable variational states.

The HB scheme applies directly to many two dimensional fermionic models, as well as to three dimensional lattices and quantum chemistry problems. Crucially, its expressive power is systematically improvable by simply increasing the path depth KK, offering a new framework with interpretability for large-scale simulations of strongly correlated fermions.

I End matter

Variational parameters in the HB. The HB wavefunction is built from elementary variational tensors fm[l]​(i,si,j,sj)f_{m}^{[l]}(i,s_{i};j,s_{j}) according to Eq. (5). Here we take K=2K=2 as an illustration,

ψmHB​(i,𝐬¯)|K=2=∑j,pfm[1]​(i,si,j,sj)​fm[2]​(j,sj,p,sp),\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\big|_{K=2}=\sum_{j,p}f_{m}^{[1]}(i,s_{i};j,s_{j})\,f_{m}^{[2]}(j,s_{j};p,s_{p}), (9)

where jj runs over sites nearby ii (typically including the site itself and its four nearest neighbors on a square lattice, giving z=5z=5 possible jj values), and pp runs over sites nearby jj. All spin indices in the ff tensors (including sis_{i}, sps_{p} and sjs_{j}) are directly specified by the configuration |𝐬⟩|{\bf s}\rangle, taking one of four possibilities for spinful fermions: |0⟩|0\rangle, |↑⟩|\uparrow\rangle, |↓⟩|\downarrow\rangle, or |↑↓⟩|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle.

In practice, the sums are evaluated on the fly according to |𝐬⟩|\mathbf{s}\rangle, and the resulting matrix Ψm​iHB=ψmHB​(i,𝐬¯)\Psi_{mi}^{\mathrm{HB}}=\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is used to compute W⁡(𝐬)=det(ΨHB)W(\mathbf{s})=\det(\Psi^{\mathrm{HB}}). The total number of variational parameters scales as z​d2​M​N​Kzd^{2}MNK, where d=4d=4 is the local Hilbert space dimension, MM the number of electrons, and NN the total number of lattice sites.

RHB as a compact representation. In the RHB, the neural network only needs to output MM values per determinant to form the Slater determinant in combination with the HB(see Figure 5). Thus, the parameter count scales as O⁡(Nneuron​M)+O⁡(M​N)O(N_{\text{neuron}}M)+O(MN), where the first term comes from the neural network and the second from the HB backbone. Here NneuronN_{\text{neuron}} is the number of hidden neurons that directly connects to the MM outputs (each connection contributes parameters).

In contrast, conventional global network architectures require O⁡(M​N)O(MN) output values to construct each Slater determinant [33, 34, 31], leading to a parameter scaling of O⁡(Nneuron​M​N)O(N_{\text{neuron}}MN). Typically M∝NM\propto N (e.g., M=78​NM=\frac{7}{8}N for hole doping nh=0.125n_{h}=0.125). Hence, for the same number of determinants which provides similar expressive power, the RHB ansatz has a favorable scaling: O⁡(Nneuron​N)+O⁡(N2)O(N_{\text{neuron}}N)+O(N^{2}) versus O⁡(Nneuron​N2)O(N_{\text{neuron}}N^{2}) for global architectures.

II Supplemental Material

II.1 1. Expressivity of backflow wavefunction

The backflow wavefunction originates from the concept of backflow corrections introduced by Feynman and Cohen to describe liquid helium [11]. It incorporates correlations by making the single-particle orbitals depend on the configuration of all other particles, providing a compelling way to improve upon mean-field Slater determinants in fermionic systems [41, 40], which has proven promising in studying various strongly correlated systems [33, 34, 31]. Generally, along a chosen site ii, the amplitude for the configuration |𝐬⟩|\bf s\rangle of a single-determinant backflow ansatz can be expressed as

W⁡(𝐬)=det(Ψ⁡(𝐬))=∑mψm​(i,𝐬¯)​Cm​(i,𝐬¯),W(\mathbf{s})=\det(\Psi({\bf s}))=\sum_{m}\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\,C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}), (10)

where the matrix element Ψm​i=ψm​(i,𝐬¯)\Psi_{mi}=\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is the backflow-corrected orbital, Cm​(i,𝐬¯)C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is the corresponding (m,i)(m,i)-cofactor of the matrix Ψ\Psi, and mm labels the orbital which ranges from 11 to particle number MM. In contrast to the Hartree-Fock approach, where orbitals depend only on the coordinates of a single particle, the backflow wavefunction is much more expressive where each orbital ψm​(i,𝐬¯)\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) depends on the occupied site ii and the full background configuration |𝐬¯⟩|\bar{\mathbf{s}}\rangle of the remaining M−1M-1 particles. Each pair (i,𝐬¯)(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) uniquely labels a configuration 𝐬\mathbf{s}.

The Jastrow-Slater wavefunction [19] is an expressive way to study correlated systems such as fractional quantum Hall effects [8] and electron structures [17]. We show that it can also be written as a single-determinant backflow wavefunction.

A Jastrow-Slater wavefunction takes the form

WJastrow​(𝐬)=eJ⁡(𝐬)​det(ΨHF),W_{\mathrm{Jastrow}}(\mathbf{s})=e^{J(\mathbf{s})}\,\det\bigl(\Psi^{\mathrm{HF}}\bigr), (11)

where Ψm​iHF=ψmHF​(i)\Psi^{\mathrm{HF}}_{mi}=\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HF}}(i) are Hartree-Fock orbitals. Expanding the determinant along an arbitrary occupied site ii yields

WJastrow​(𝐬)=eJ⁡(𝐬)​∑mψmHF​(i)​CmHF​(i,𝐬¯),W_{\mathrm{Jastrow}}(\mathbf{s})=e^{J(\mathbf{s})}\sum_{m}\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HF}}(i)\,C_{m}^{\mathrm{HF}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}), (12)

where CmHFC_{m}^{\mathrm{HF}} is the corresponding cofactor. Since eJ⁡(𝐬)=[eJ⁡(𝐬)/M]Me^{J(\mathbf{s})}=[e^{J(\mathbf{s})/M}]^{M}, for an MM-particle system, we may absorb the Jastrow factor into a redefinition of the orbitals:

ψ~m​(i,𝐬¯)=eJ⁡(𝐬)/M​ψmHF​(i).\tilde{\psi}_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})=e^{J(\mathbf{s})/M}\,\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HF}}(i). (13)

Then the matrix Ψ~\tilde{\Psi} with elements Ψ~m​i=ψ~m​(i,𝐬¯)\tilde{\Psi}_{mi}=\tilde{\psi}_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) satisfies WJastrow​(𝐬)=det(Ψ~)W_{\rm Jastrow}(\mathbf{s})=\det(\tilde{\Psi}). Thus in this sense, a Jastrow-Slater wavefunction could be regarded as a special case of the backflow wavefunction.

II.2 2. Single-particle-like effective Hamiltonian for the backflow wavefunction

Here we show how to motivate a single-particle-like eigenvalue problem with an effective Hamiltonian. We consider a fermionic Hubbard-type Hamiltonian

H=∑⟨i​j⟩ti​j​ci†​cj+∑⟨i​k⟩Ui​k​ni​nk,H=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}t_{ij}\,c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}+\sum_{\langle ik\rangle}U_{ik}\,n_{i}n_{k}, (14)

acting on Fock states |𝐬⟩|\mathbf{s}\rangle with occupation numbers ni=ci†​cin_{i}=c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{i}. For an MM-electron system, a general wavefunction is |Φ⟩=∑𝐬W⁡(𝐬)​|𝐬⟩|\Phi\rangle=\sum_{\mathbf{s}}W(\mathbf{s})|\mathbf{s}\rangle. The amplitude of the backflow wavefunction W⁡(𝐬)W(\mathbf{s}) can be expressed by expanding the determinant along the ii-th column for any occupied site ii,

W⁡(𝐬)=det(Ψ)=∑mψm​(i,𝐬¯)​Cm​(i,𝐬¯),W(\mathbf{s})=\det(\Psi)=\sum_{m}\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}), (15)

where 𝐬¯\bar{\mathbf{s}} (depending on ii) denotes the background configuration of the remaining electrons after removing the particle at site ii from 𝐬\mathbf{s}. The matrix element Ψm​i=ψm​(i,𝐬¯)\Psi_{mi}=\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is the backflow-corrected orbital, Cm​(i,𝐬¯)C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is the corresponding (m,i)(m,i)-cofactor of the matrix Ψ\Psi, and mm labels the orbitals (m=1,…,Mm=1,\dots,M). In contrast to the Hartree-Fock approach, where orbitals depend only on single-particle coordinates, here each orbital ψm​(i,𝐬¯)\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) depends on the full background configuration of the remaining electrons.

We take the backflow-corrected orbital values ψm​(i,𝐬¯)\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) as variational parameters. The energy expectation value is E=⟨Φ|H|Φ⟩/⟨Φ|Φ⟩E=\langle\Phi|H|\Phi\rangle/\langle\Phi|\Phi\rangle. Varying ψm​(i,𝐬¯)\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) and imposing δ​E=0\delta E=0 then yields the variational condition:

⟨δ​Φδ​ψm​(i,𝐬¯)|H−E|Φ⟩=0.\langle\frac{\delta\Phi}{\delta\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}|H-E|\Phi\rangle=0. (16)

Because ∂W⁡(𝐬)/∂ψm​(i,𝐬¯)=Cm​(i,𝐬¯)\partial W(\mathbf{s})/\partial\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})=C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}), the left-hand side of the variational condition can be expanded as

⟨δ​Φδ​ψm​(i,𝐬¯)|H−E|Φ⟩=∑𝐬′∂W⁡(𝐬′)∂ψm​(i,𝐬¯)​⟨𝐬′|H−E|Φ⟩=Cm​(i,𝐬¯)​⟨𝐬​|H−E|​Φ⟩.\langle\frac{\delta\Phi}{\delta\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}|H-E|\Phi\rangle=\sum_{\mathbf{s}^{\prime}}\frac{\partial W(\mathbf{s}^{\prime})}{\partial\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}\langle\mathbf{s}^{\prime}|H-E|\Phi\rangle=C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\langle\mathbf{s}|H-E|\Phi\rangle. (17)

The pair (i,𝐬¯)(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) determines the full configuration 𝐬\mathbf{s} uniquely. Hence ∂W⁡(𝐬′)/∂ψm​(i,𝐬¯)\partial W(\mathbf{s}^{\prime})/\partial\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is nonzero only for 𝐬′=𝐬\mathbf{s}^{\prime}=\mathbf{s}. Here we implicitly restrict to configurations with Cm​(i,𝐬¯)≠0C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\neq 0, as others give vanishing contributions.

Consequently, we obtain the equation

⟨𝐬|H|Φ⟩=E⁡⟨𝐬|Φ⟩,∀𝐬.\langle\mathbf{s}|H|\Phi\rangle=E\langle\mathbf{s}|\Phi\rangle,\qquad\forall\mathbf{s}. (18)

Expanding this equation gives

⟨𝐬|H|Φ⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{s}|H|\Phi\rangle =∑𝐬′W⁡(𝐬′)​⟨𝐬|H|𝐬′⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{s}^{\prime}}W(\mathbf{s}^{\prime})\langle\mathbf{s}|H|\mathbf{s}^{\prime}\rangle (19)
=∑⟨i​j⟩ti​j​∑𝐬′W⁡(𝐬′)​⟨𝐬|ci†​cj​|𝐬′⟩+∑⟨i​k⟩Ui​k​∑𝐬′W⁡(𝐬′)​⟨𝐬|​ni​nk|𝐬′⟩.\displaystyle=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}t_{ij}\sum_{\mathbf{s}^{\prime}}W(\mathbf{s}^{\prime})\langle\mathbf{s}|c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}|\mathbf{s}^{\prime}\rangle+\sum_{\langle ik\rangle}U_{ik}\sum_{\mathbf{s}^{\prime}}W(\mathbf{s}^{\prime})\langle\mathbf{s}|n_{i}n_{k}|\mathbf{s}^{\prime}\rangle.

The hopping matrix element is nonzero only when 𝐬′=𝐬−i+j\mathbf{s}^{\prime}=\mathbf{s}_{-i+j}, the configuration obtained by moving one electron from site ii to site jj in 𝐬\mathbf{s} (if the move is allowed; otherwise the term vanishes), as illustrated in Figure 6. We define for the hopping term

ηi​jh​(𝐬¯)=∑𝐬′⟨𝐬|ci†​cj|𝐬′⟩,\eta_{ij}^{\mathrm{h}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})=\sum_{\mathbf{s}^{\prime}}\langle\mathbf{s}|c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}|\mathbf{s}^{\prime}\rangle, (20)

which equals the sign factor ±1\pm 1 if the move is allowed, and 00 otherwise. Similarly, for the interaction term

ηi​kI​(𝐬¯)=∑𝐬′⟨𝐬|ni​nk|𝐬′⟩.\eta_{ik}^{\mathrm{I}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})=\sum_{\mathbf{s}^{\prime}}\langle\mathbf{s}|n_{i}n_{k}|\mathbf{s}^{\prime}\rangle. (21)

Both ηi​jh\eta_{ij}^{\mathrm{h}} and ηi​kI\eta_{ik}^{\mathrm{I}} depend only on the configuration 𝐬\mathbf{s}, or equivalently on the pair (i,𝐬¯)(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}).

Using the Kronecker delta δi​j\delta_{ij} to combine the two sums into a single sum over i,ji,j, we obtain

⟨𝐬|H|Φ⟩=∑i​jW⁡(𝐬−i+j)​(ti​j​ηi​jh​(𝐬¯)+δi​j​∑kUj​k​ηj​kI​(𝐬¯))=E​W​(𝐬).\langle\mathbf{s}|H|\Phi\rangle=\sum_{ij}W(\mathbf{s}_{-i+j})\Bigl(t_{ij}\eta_{ij}^{\mathrm{h}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})+\delta_{ij}\sum_{k}U_{jk}\eta_{jk}^{\mathrm{I}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\Bigr)=EW(\mathbf{s}). (22)

where the sum over jj includes site ii and its neighbors (for the hopping terms), and the sum over kk includes the neighbors of site ii (for the interaction terms).

For an exact eigenstate, the equation ⟨𝐬|H|Φ⟩=E​W​(𝐬)\langle\mathbf{s}|H|\Phi\rangle=EW(\mathbf{s}) must hold for every 𝐬\mathbf{s}. This condition alone, however, does not uniquely determine the individual variational terms. To get a tractable set of equations that can inspire a flexible variational ansatz, we introduce auxiliary quantities Eloc​(i,𝐬¯)E^{\mathrm{loc}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) for each occupied site ii and the background configuration 𝐬¯\bar{\mathbf{s}}, defined as

Eloc​(i,𝐬¯)=∑jW⁡(𝐬−i+j)W⁡(𝐬)​(ti​j​ηi​jh​(𝐬¯)+δi​j​∑kUj​k​ηj​kI​(𝐬¯)).E^{\mathrm{loc}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})=\sum_{j}\frac{W(\mathbf{s}_{-i+j})}{W(\mathbf{s})}\Bigl(t_{ij}\eta_{ij}^{\mathrm{h}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})+\delta_{ij}\sum_{k}U_{jk}\eta_{jk}^{\mathrm{I}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\Bigr). (23)

This definition closely parallels the concept of the local energy Eloc​(𝐬)=⟨𝐬|H|Φ⟩/W⁡(𝐬)E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{s})=\langle\mathbf{s}|H|\Phi\rangle/W(\mathbf{s}) commonly used in the scheme of variational Monte Carlo; see Eq.(31). In VMC, one typically estimates the global energy as the average of Eloc​(𝐬)E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{s}) over sampled configurations. Here we decompose the local energy into site-resolved contributions: Eloc​(𝐬)=∑iEloc​(i,𝐬¯)E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{s})=\sum_{i}E^{\mathrm{loc}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}), where the sum runs over all occupied sites ii in 𝐬\mathbf{s}. This decomposition is natural because the Hamiltonian consists of single-site (potential) and two-site (hopping) terms, each of which can be associated with specific sites. Since for an exact eigenstate Eloc​(𝐬)=EE_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{s})=E for all 𝐬\mathbf{s}, summing Eloc​(i,𝐬¯)E^{\mathrm{loc}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) over all occupied sites ii in a given configuration 𝐬\mathbf{s} can yield the total energy EE.

Expanding the determinant W⁡(𝐬−i+j)=det(Ψ⁡(𝐬−i+j))W(\mathbf{s}_{-i+j})=\det(\Psi(\mathbf{s}_{-i+j})) along the mm-th row (for a fixed mm) yields, for each mm,

W⁡(𝐬−i+j)=ψm​(j,𝐬¯)​Cm​(j,𝐬¯)⏟Am​(j,𝐬¯)+∑p≠jψm​(p,𝐬[p])​Cm​(p,𝐬[p])⏟Bm​(j,𝐬¯),W(\mathbf{s}_{-i+j})=\underbrace{\psi_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})C_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}_{\displaystyle A_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}\;+\;\underbrace{\sum_{p\neq j}\psi_{m}(p,\mathbf{s}^{[p]})C_{m}(p,\mathbf{s}^{[p]})}_{\displaystyle B_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}, (24)

where 𝐬¯\bar{\mathbf{s}} is the background configuration obtained by removing the particle at site ii from the original configuration 𝐬\mathbf{s}, and 𝐬[p]\mathbf{s}^{[p]} denotes the background obtained by removing the particle at site pp from 𝐬−i+j\mathbf{s}_{-i+j}. Here, Am​(j,𝐬¯)A_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) corresponds to the term where the expanded site jj has the same background 𝐬¯\bar{\mathbf{s}} as the original reference, while Bm​(j,𝐬¯)B_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) collects all contributions from other sites p≠jp\neq j with different backgrounds 𝐬[p]\mathbf{s}^{[p]}.

To isolate the contributions from the AmA_{m} terms, we substitute the full expansion of W⁡(𝐬−i+j)W(\mathbf{s}_{-i+j}) and W⁡(𝐬)W(\mathbf{s}) from Eq. (24) into Eq. (23) and collect all terms that contain Am​(j,𝐬¯)A_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) on the left-hand side. Moving all other terms to the right-hand side, we obtain

∑jAm​(j,𝐬¯)​(ti​j​ηi​jh​(𝐬¯)+δi​j​∑kUj​k​ηj​kI​(𝐬¯))−Eloc​(i,𝐬¯)​Am​(i,𝐬¯)=Rm​(i,𝐬¯),\sum_{j}A_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\Bigl(t_{ij}\eta_{ij}^{\mathrm{h}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})+\delta_{ij}\sum_{k}U_{jk}\eta_{jk}^{\mathrm{I}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\Bigr)-E^{\mathrm{loc}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})A_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})=R_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}), (25)

where Rm​(i,𝐬¯)R_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) denotes the remainder that contains all contributions arising from the terms with different background configurations in Eq. (24). Explicitly,

Rm(i,𝐬¯)=−∑jBm(j,𝐬¯)(ti​jηi​jh(𝐬¯)+δi​j∑kUj​kηj​kI(𝐬¯))+Eloc(i,𝐬¯)Bm(i,𝐬¯).R_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})=-\!\!\sum_{j}B_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\Bigl(t_{ij}\eta_{ij}^{\mathrm{h}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})+\delta_{ij}\sum_{k}U_{jk}\eta_{jk}^{\mathrm{I}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\Bigr)+E^{\mathrm{loc}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})B_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}). (26)

To obtain an effective single-particle-like description, we define

εm​(i,𝐬¯)=Rm​(i,𝐬¯)ψm​(i,𝐬¯)​Cm​(i,𝐬¯),\varepsilon_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})=\frac{R_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}{\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\,C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}, (27)

which formally expresses the original multi-configuration variational condition as a set of single-particle-like equations.

With this we have

∑jψm​(j,𝐬¯)​Cm​(j,𝐬¯)​(ti​j​ηi​jh​(𝐬¯)+δi​j​∑kUj​k​ηj​kI​(𝐬¯))=[Eloc​(i,𝐬¯)+εm​(i,𝐬¯)]​ψm​(i,𝐬¯)​Cm​(i,𝐬¯).\sum_{j}\psi_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})C_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\left(t_{ij}\eta^{\mathrm{h}}_{ij}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})+\delta_{ij}\sum_{k}U_{jk}\eta^{\mathrm{I}}_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\right)=\left[E^{\mathrm{loc}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})+\varepsilon_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})\right]\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}). (28)

We perform an additional reparametrization, setting Eloc​(i,𝐬¯)+εm​(i,𝐬¯)=Em​(𝐬¯)​γm​(i,𝐬¯)E^{\mathrm{loc}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})+\varepsilon_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})=E_{m}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\gamma_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}), where Em​(𝐬¯)E_{m}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}) plays the role of the eigenvalue for the effective Hamiltonian, and γm​(i,𝐬¯)\gamma_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is a non-zero scaling factor that could be formally absorbed into the Hamiltonian matrix elements. Eventually, we could obtain an effective Hamiltonian:

∑j[Hmeff​(𝐬¯)]i​j​ψm​(j,𝐬¯)=Em​(𝐬¯)​ψm​(i,𝐬¯),\sum_{j}\left[H_{m}^{\mathrm{eff}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\right]_{ij}\psi_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})=E_{m}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\psi_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}), (29)

where the effective Hamiltonian elements read

[Hmeff​(𝐬¯)]i​j=1γm​(i,𝐬¯)​Cm​(j,𝐬¯)Cm​(i,𝐬¯)​(ti​j​ηi​jh​(𝐬¯)+δi​j​∑kUj​k​ηj​kI​(𝐬¯)).\left[H_{m}^{\mathrm{eff}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\right]_{ij}=\frac{1}{\gamma_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}\frac{C_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}{C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})}\left(t_{ij}\eta^{\mathrm{h}}_{ij}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})+\delta_{ij}\sum_{k}U_{jk}\eta^{\mathrm{I}}_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf{s}})\right). (30)

We note the above construction should be viewed as a heuristic derivation for an effective single-particle-like Hamiltonian. The effective Hamiltonian is in general nonlinear and computationally challenging. For each background configuration 𝐬¯\bar{\mathbf{s}} and orbital mm, the effective Hamiltonian Hmeff​(𝐬¯)H_{m}^{\mathrm{eff}}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}) depends on the cofactor ratio Cm​(j,𝐬¯)/Cm​(i,𝐬¯)C_{m}(j,\bar{\mathbf{s}})/C_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}), which itself is a function of the orbitals across different backgrounds, and the scaling factor γm​(i,𝐬¯)\gamma_{m}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is also not predetermined. Consequently, solving these equations directly by iteration is impractical. Instead, the effective Hamiltonian motivates the path-expansion ansatz, which we then treat as a variational wavefunction and perform practical calculations within the scheme of variational Monte Carlo.

II.3 3. Optimization with variational Monte Carlo

We use the variational Monte Carlo (VMC) for optimization. In VMC, the energy function and the pp-th parameter’s gradient are evaluated through the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method:

E=⟨Φ|H|Φ⟩⟨Φ|Φ⟩=∑𝐬W​(𝐬)2​⟨𝐬|H|Φ⟩W⁡(𝐬)=⟨Eloc​(𝐬)⟩,gp=2​⟨Eloc​(𝐬)​Op​(𝐬)⟩−2​⟨Eloc​(𝐬)⟩​⟨Op​(𝐬)⟩,\begin{split}&E=\frac{\langle\Phi|H|\Phi\rangle}{\langle\Phi|\Phi\rangle}=\sum_{\mathbf{s}}W(\mathbf{s})^{2}\frac{\langle{\bf s}|H|\Phi\rangle}{W({\bf s})}=\langle E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{s})\rangle,\\ &g_{p}=2\langle E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{s})O_{p}(\mathbf{s})\rangle-2\langle E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{s})\rangle\langle O_{p}(\mathbf{s})\rangle,\end{split} (31)

where the local energy is Eloc​(𝐬)=⟨𝐬|H|Φ⟩W⁡(𝐬)=∑𝐬′W⁡(𝐬′)W⁡(𝐬)​⟨𝐬′|H|𝐬⟩E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{s})=\frac{\langle{\bf s}|H|\Phi\rangle}{W({\bf s})}=\sum_{\mathbf{s}^{\prime}}\frac{W(\mathbf{s}^{\prime})}{W(\mathbf{s})}\langle\mathbf{s}^{\prime}|H|\mathbf{s}\rangle, the Op​(𝐬)=1W⁡(𝐬)​∂W⁡(𝐬)∂xpO_{p}(\mathbf{s})=\frac{1}{W(\mathbf{s})}\frac{\partial W(\mathbf{s})}{\partial x_{p}}, and ⟨⋯⟩\langle\cdots\rangle denotes the average on MCMC samples. gpg_{p} is the energy gradients with respect to the pp-th parameters xpx_{p}.

For optimization we employ the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) method [38, 30], which is equivalent to the imaginary time evolution using the time-dependent variational principle. SR requires solving the linear system:

∑qSp​q​x˙q=gp,\sum_{q}S_{pq}\dot{x}_{q}=g_{p}, (32)

where Sp​q=⟨Op​Oq⟩−⟨Op⟩​⟨Oq⟩S_{pq}=\langle O_{p}O_{q}\rangle-\langle O_{p}\rangle\langle O_{q}\rangle. To avoid explicitly constructing the SS matrix, we solve the above equation in an iterative way and we only need to know how to map a vector x˙\dot{x} to yy under action SS to realize y=S​x˙y=S\dot{x}. Specifically,

yp=∑qSp​q​x˙q=yp(1)−yp(2),y_{p}=\sum_{q}S_{pq}\dot{x}_{q}=y_{p}^{(1)}-y_{p}^{(2)}, (33)

where

yp(1)\displaystyle y_{p}^{(1)} =1NMC​∑𝐬Op​(𝐬)​[∑qOq​(𝐬)​x˙q],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{\text{MC}}}\sum_{\mathbf{s}}O_{p}(\mathbf{s})\left[\sum_{q}O_{q}(\mathbf{s})\dot{x}_{q}\right], (34)
yp(2)\displaystyle y_{p}^{(2)} =⟨Op​(𝐬)⟩​∑qOq​(𝐬)​x˙q,\displaystyle=\langle O_{p}(\mathbf{s})\rangle\sum_{q}O_{q}(\mathbf{s})\dot{x}_{q},

where NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}} is the number of Monte Carlo samples, which is about 1600016000 in our calculations. Note Op​(𝐬)O_{p}(\mathbf{s}) can be stored trivially on different CPU processors, while still being convenient to iteratively solve the equation. In practice, we add a small diagonal regularization (e.g., ϵ=10−3\epsilon=10^{-3}) to SS to ensure numerical stability. Once x˙\dot{x} is obtained, parameters are updated as

xp​(τ+1)=xp​(τ)−d​τ⋅x˙p,x_{p}(\tau+1)=x_{p}(\tau)-d\tau\cdot\dot{x}_{p}, (35)

where d​τd\tau is the step size, which can be tuned from d​τ=0.1d\tau=0.1 to 0.010.01.

For the residual hierarchical backflow (RHB) wavefunction using NdetN_{\det} determinants, its amplitude W⁡(𝐬)W(\mathbf{s}) is obtained according to

W⁡(𝐬)=∑α=1Ndetdet(Ψ[α]),W(\mathbf{s})=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{N_{\det}}\det(\Psi^{[\alpha]}), (36)

with matrix elements

Ψm​i[α]=ψmHB​(i,𝐬¯)​Qm[α]​(𝐬¯).\Psi^{[\alpha]}_{mi}=\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}})Q_{m}^{[\alpha]}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}). (37)

All determinant share the same orbitals ψmHB\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}} but each carries its own configuration-dependent factor Qm[α]​(𝐬¯)Q_{m}^{[\alpha]}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}) that can be parameterized by a neural network. This multi-determinant construction, with independent Qm[α]​(𝐬¯)Q_{m}^{[\alpha]}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}) factors, lifts the single-determinant constraint and provides additional variational freedom beyond the HB backbone, thereby enhancing the expressive power.

The hierarchical part ψmHB​(i,𝐬¯)\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}(i,\bar{\mathbf{s}}) is directly computed as in the HB wavefunction. For the nonlocal part Qm[α]​(𝐬¯)Q_{m}^{[\alpha]}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}), for simplicity we adopt a three-layer fully connected feed-forward neural network (FNN) for the spinful case, as illustrated in Figure 7(a). The network is described as follow:

  1. 1.

    Input Layer: The input layer consists of 2​N2N neurons encoding the configuration |𝐬¯⟩|\bar{\mathbf{s}}\rangle, which is obtained from |𝐬⟩|\mathbf{s}\rangle by removing the electron at site ii. For each site ii, two neurons (ia,ib)(i_{a},i_{b}) represent the spin-up and spin-down components, respectively. Neuron iai_{a} outputs +1+1 if site ii is occupied by a spin-up electron and −1-1 otherwise; neuron ibi_{b} outputs +1+1 if site ii is occupied by a spin-down electron and −1-1 otherwise.

  2. 2.

    Hidden Layer: The hidden layer contains NneuronN_{\text{neuron}} neurons with the Sigmoid Linear Unit (SiLU) activation function, SiLU⁡(x)=x⋅sigmoid⁡(x)=x/(1+e−x)\mathrm{SiLU}(x)=x\cdot\mathrm{sigmoid}(x)=x/(1+e^{-x}).

  3. 3.

    Output Layer: The output layer contains Ndet×MN_{\text{det}}\times M neurons, each with a linear activation function, outputting the values of the nonlocal factors Qm[α]​(𝐬¯)Q_{m}^{[\alpha]}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}) for each orbital mm and determinant α\alpha.

The neural network introduces variational parameters from the two fully connected layers, totaling approximately 4​Nneuron​N+2​Ndet​Nneuron​M4N_{\text{neuron}}N+2N_{\text{det}}N_{\text{neuron}}M (including both weights and biases). The HB part contributes z​d2​K​M​Nzd^{2}KMN parameters. Hence, the total number of variational parameters in the RHB wavefunction scales as O⁡(Nneuron​N)+O⁡(Nneuron​M)+O⁡(M​N)O(N_{\text{neuron}}N)+O(N_{\text{neuron}}M)+O(MN). In this work, we typically set Nneuron=100N_{\text{neuron}}=100 and Ndet=5N_{\text{det}}=5 (see later).

The local-nonlocal structure of the RHB enables a two-stage optimization. Concretely, we first optimize the HB backbone alone (take K=2K=2), then introduce the nonlocal factor Qm[α]​(𝐬¯)Q_{m}^{[\alpha]}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}) and perform a joint optimization of both the HB and the nonlocal part. Figure 7(b) compares the optimization behavior using different schemes for the 4×164\times 16 Hubbard model at U=8U=8 and hole doping nh=0.125n_{h}=0.125. In the naive optimization, the RHB ansatz (including the FNN) is optimized directly from the Hartree-Fock starting point. The energy converges slowly and becomes trapped at a relatively high value. In contrast, using the two-stage scheme enabled by the local-nonlocal structure, we first optimize the HB backbone; this converges rapidly and already reaches an energy lower than that of the naive full optimization. We then add the FNN and continue joint optimization, which further lowers the energy significantly below the naive result. This demonstrates the advantage of the local-nonlocal structure of RHB for efficient and accurate simulations.

II.4 4. Additional Results

Table 2 presents energy comparisons for cases of half filling on the square lattice under PBC. The reference energies are from auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) without sign problems [35]. From the table, the K=1K=1 wavefunction reproduces the AFQMC energies with remarkable accuracy, achieving relative errors on the order of 10−310^{-3} across all cases.

Table 3 shows the ground-state energy per site for the 4×44\times 4 Hubbard model at nh=0.125n_{h}=0.125, U=8U=8. The HB K=2K=2 energy is −0.7385-0.7385. With the RHB ansatz using Ndet=5N_{\mathrm{det}}=5 determinants and Nneuron=100N_{\mathrm{neuron}}=100, the energy improves to −0.7403-0.7403, corresponding to a relative error of 2×10−32\times 10^{-3} compared to the exact diagonalization (ED) result −0.7418-0.7418. Increasing NdetN_{\mathrm{det}} to 1616 (with Nneuron=80N_{\mathrm{neuron}}=80) further reduces the error to 1.1×10−31.1\times 10^{-3}, but at a higher computational cost. Based on this tradeoff, we adopt Ndet=5N_{\mathrm{det}}=5 and Nneuron=100N_{\mathrm{neuron}}=100 for all subsequent large-scale simulations.

Table 4 compares the ground-state energies for 4×L4\times L rectangular lattices at hole doping nh=0.125n_{h}=0.125 and U=8U=8 under PBC. Reference energies are from NNB [33] and HFDS [34]. NNB replaces the static set of orbitals with a configuration dependent set which is generated by a neural network. HFDS instead works in the paradigm of projected hidden fermions using neural networks to replace the standard Slater Determinant with a larger determinant which includes single-particle orbitals. The two methods have intrinsic relations [31].

We also compare the local spin moment ⟨Sz⟩\langle S^{z}\rangle and the hole density distributions for the 4×164\times 16 lattice at nh=0.125n_{h}=0.125. Figure 8 shows that the distributions obtained with K=1K=1, K=2K=2, and the RHB are nearly identical. This indicates that the essential spatial structure of spin and charge is already captured by the hierarchical backflow component ψmHB\psi_{m}^{\mathrm{HB}}, and the nonlocal factor Qm[α]​(𝐬¯)Q_{m}^{[\alpha]}(\bar{\mathbf{s}}) in this case primarily provides an energy refinement.
